readmeExcerpt:
The cost reduction engine for AI coding agents.
Install it and forget it, then go as far as you want with pipelines.

Install • Pipelines • Docs • Website • RTK Pro • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português


**① Install & forget: up to 90% less command output.** Test runs, diffs, logs and builds are compressed before your agent reads them. 100+ commands, under 25 ms per command, no config, nothing changes in how you work. `rtk gain` shows what you saved. **② Go further with pipelines, as far as you take it.** Hand heavy reads to a cheaper model, compress more than bash, clean the API traffic without breaking the prompt cache. One agent-agnostic file: start from a built-in, install one someone shared, or write and share your own. The community built the bash compressor 85k developers starred. Now it is building pipelines: the best one listed today cuts total cost by 20.2% in its [author's benchmark](https://www.rtk-ai.app/pipelines/). **Agents across the whole company?** [RTK Pro](https://pro.rtk-ai.app) is the control layer for every AI agent: one gateway for every AI call, costs, secrets and personal data, policies, team catalog, audit. [Discover RTK Pro ↓](#agents-across-the-whole-company-know-what-they-cost-what-they-touch-and-who-ran-what)


---
## Install & forget **macOS, and Linux with Homebrew** ```bash brew install rtk ``` **Windows, with winget** ```bash winget install rtk-ai.rtk ``` **Linux, macOS or WSL, with the install script** ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh ``` **Then plug it into your agent** ```bash rtk init -g # Claude Code; every other agent: see "Works in your agent" ``` Restart your agent. That's it: when it runs `git status`, RTK runs `rtk git status` and the agent reads a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. Nothing to learn, nothing to call, and upgrading RTK never changes this. > Another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io. Check you have this one: `rtk gain` must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found". > > Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL and uninstall: **[Installation guide](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/installation/)** · per-agent setup and `--dry-run`: **[Quick Start](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/quick-start/)**
## Measure it: `rtk gain` Every command RTK touches is counted on your machine. One command shows what it saved, today and since you installed it. ```bash rtk gain # Summary stats rtk gain --graph # ASCII graph (last 30 days) rtk gain --history # Recent command history rtk gain --daily # Day-by-day breakdown rtk gain --all --format json # JSON export for dashboards rtk discover # Find missed savings opportunities rtk discover --all --since 7 # All projects, last 7 days rtk session # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions ``` **What the numbers mean.** The compressor reduces the **command output** your agent reads, which is one part of the input tokens, which are one part of the bill: a 90% cut in command output is not a 90% cut in cost. Token counts are estimated as `bytes / 4`, so the percentages are reliable and the absolute numbers are approximate. After a week of data, `rtk gain` ends with one line about RTK Pro, at most once a day and only on a terminal. `pro_hint = false` under `[display]` in `config.toml` turns it off. > Full explanation: [How RTK Savings Work](docs/guide/resources/savings-explained.md) · attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: **[Token Savings Analytics](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/analytics/gain/)**
## Out of the box: the bash compressor The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship.

| Operation | What the agent reads | |-----------|----------------------| | `cargo test` / `npm test` / `pytest` / `go test` | Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count | | `git status` / `git diff` / `git log` | Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit | | `git add/commit/push` | A confirmation line instead of progress output | | `ls` / `tree` / `grep` / `rg` | Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut | | `ruff check` / `eslint` / `cargo clippy` | Grouped by rule and file | | `docker ps` / `kubectl` | Essential fields only | 100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: **[What RTK Optimizes](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/what-rtk-covers/)** **Three promises** - **Never blocks.** If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged. - **Never worse.** RTK never prints more than the command did. - **Nothing hidden.** Output that is cut says where the full version is, and `rtk bypass` runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in `rtk gain`: ```bash rtk bypass git log --oneline -20 # full git log, no truncation rtk bypass npm install express # raw npm output ``` The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see [Pipelines](#want-to-go-further-pipelines) below). > **Does RTK break the prompt cache?** No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. [Details](docs/guide/resources/troubleshooting.md#does-rtk-break-claudes-prompt-cache).
## Want to go further? Pipelines. Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out.

**What people turn on first** - **Compress everything the agent reads**, not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code). - **Hand big file reads to a cheaper model** you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key). - **Clean the API traffic** your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below). - **Make the agent write less**: terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent). Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. **[rtk-ai.app/pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/pipelines/)** lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command: ```bash rtk pipeline add github:user/repo # check and install a shared pipeline ``` A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: **[Agent Coverage](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/agent-coverage/)** shows what runs where. > Start here: **[Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/overview/)** · the built-ins, explained: **[Reference Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/reference-pipelines/)** · write and share your own: **[Writing a Pipeline](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/writing-pipelines/)**, **[Pipeline Commands](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/commands/)** ### RTK Proxy (optional) The `rtk-proxy` daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's **provider-API traffic**: it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in `rtk gain`. `rtk init -g` offer

Out of the box: the bash compressor

The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship.

Operation What the agent reads
cargo test / npm test / pytest / go test Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count
git status / git diff / git log Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit
git add/commit/push A confirmation line instead of progress output
ls / tree / grep / rg Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut
ruff check / eslint / cargo clippy Grouped by rule and file
docker ps / kubectl Essential fields only

100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: What RTK Optimizes

Three promises

  • Never blocks. If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged.
  • Never worse. RTK never prints more than the command did.
  • Nothing hidden. Output that is cut says where the full version is, and rtk bypass runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in rtk gain:
rtk bypass git log --oneline -20        # full git log, no truncation
rtk bypass npm install express          # raw npm output

The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as Read, Grep and Glob pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see Pipelines below).

Does RTK break the prompt cache? No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. Details.


Want to go further? Pipelines.

Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out.

What people turn on first

  • Compress everything the agent reads, not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code).
  • Hand big file reads to a cheaper model you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key).
  • Clean the API traffic your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below).
  • Make the agent write less: terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent).

Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. rtk-ai.app/pipelines lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command:

rtk pipeline add github:user/repo        # check and install a shared pipeline

A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: Agent Coverage shows what runs where.

Start here: Pipelines · the built-ins, explained: Reference Pipelines · write and share your own: Writing a Pipeline, Pipeline Commands

RTK Proxy (optional)

The rtk-proxy daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's provider-API traffic: it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in rtk gain. rtk init -g offers to set it up; rtk claude starts it and launches Claude through it with no configuration at all.

rtk claude              # start the daemon if needed, then launch Claude through it
rtk llm-proxy status    # is it up
rtk gain                # savings, command filtering and proxy side by side

Separate binary, separate licence (BUSL-1.1), its own rtk-proxy-<target> archive: rtk never links it. Not the same thing as rtk bypass, which runs one local command unfiltered.

Setup and subcommands: RTK Proxy · what it compresses: What the Proxy Compresses · settings and endpoints: Proxy Configuration

Works in your agent

RTK supports 18 AI coding tools. With a hook or plugin, rtk init installs it and compression is automatic. With a rules file, RTK asks the model to prefer rtk commands instead.

Tool Install How
Claude Code rtk init -g hook
GitHub Copilot (VS Code, CLI) rtk init -g --copilot hook
Cursor rtk init -g --agent cursor hook
Gemini CLI rtk init -g --gemini hook
Codex rtk init -g --codex hook
Mistral Vibe rtk init -g --agent vibe hook
Factory Droid rtk init -g --agent droid hook
Trae rtk init --agent trae (or -g) hook
OpenCode (1.18.29+) rtk init -g --opencode plugin
OpenClaw openclaw plugins install ./openclaw plugin
Pi / Oh My Pi rtk init -g --agent pi / --agent omp plugin
Hermes rtk init --agent hermes plugin
Windsurf rtk init -g --agent windsurf rules file
Cline / Roo Code rtk init --agent cline rules file
Kilo Code rtk init --agent kilocode rules file
Google Antigravity rtk init --agent antigravity (or -g) rules file
Kimi AI rtk init --agent kimi rules file

Editions and licence

RTK ships as three downloads. The two rtk editions install a binary with the same name — hooks, scripts and agent config work unchanged across both — so they cannot be installed together. Uninstall one before installing the other.

Download Licence Contains
rtk-<target> Apache-2.0 + BUSL-1.1 Hook core, every command filter, and the pipeline engine
rtk-oss-<target> Apache-2.0 only Hook core and every command filter. No engine.
rtk-proxy-<target> BUSL-1.1 The RTK Proxy daemon. Never bundled with either rtk.

Production use is free, engine and daemon included. What the BUSL grant does not cover is offering RTK or a derivative to third parties as a commercial product or service — for that, contact contact@rtk-ai.app.

curl -fsSL .../install.sh | RTK_EDITION=oss sh    # Apache-2.0 edition
brew install rtk-ai/tap/rtk-oss

The rtk CLI is Apache-2.0 — see LICENSE. It links one component under a different licence: rtk-engine (engine/) is BUSL-1.1, source-available: see engine/LICENSE. Its Additional Use Grant permits production use as part of the rtk binary, so running rtk is covered; using the engine on its own, or inside another product, is not until the Change Date. The rtk-proxy daemon (proxy/) is BUSL-1.1 on the same terms and ships as its own archive with its licence alongside — rtk never links it.

What the Apache-2.0 edition omits and where the licence boundary falls: Editions and Licensing

aiSummary.oneLiner: A high-performance CLI proxy written in Rust that radically compresses shell output to reduce LLM context token usage.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: rtk intercepts standard developer terminal commands and heavily filters their output before it is read by an AI coding agent, significantly reducing token consumption. The tool operates as a remarkably fast, single-binary Rust proxy with virtually zero latency overhead, capable of intelligently summarizing the output of over 100 common development tools. Instead of returning raw, verbose logs from commands like git diff or cargo test, it parses the output and returns highly dense, compacted summaries containing only the essential failure traces or structural metadata. By aggressively truncating redundant text, rtk massively accelerates agent processing times and drastically lowers API billing costs without degrading the agent's contextual awareness.
keyFeatures: Smart output compression: Intercepts verbose terminal commands automatically and rewrites them into highly compact, token-efficient summaries.
Zero dependency Rust binary: Deploys rapidly as a single, incredibly fast Rust executable adding under 10ms of overhead to standard shell commands.
Tool-specific parsing: Contains deep, native understanding for over 100 tools, intelligently extracting only failures from test runners or structural counts from directory listings.
Agent agnostic integration: Operates seamlessly alongside any standard AI coding assistant or CLI by simply acting as a transparent proxy layer.
Massive token reduction: Empirically slashes the raw bash output length ingested by the LLM by up to 90 percent on standard debugging workflows.
